summary: This RFC is an official status report on protocol parameter values in the Internet family: network numbers, well-known ports, protocol types, and version numbers. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 923.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers need agreed numbers for things, like which door to knock on for which service. This was the official list, now replaced by later lists.

questions: what were the assigned numbers in 1984
where are well known port numbers listed
how many class a networks exist
what is protocol number for icmp
subtitle: Official registry of protocol numbers, port assignments, and network identifiers

tldr.problem: Internet protocols need consistent numbering schemes for network identifiers, well-known ports, protocol types, and version numbers to ensure interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents all assigned values from several series used in network protocol implementations, including network numbers, protocol identifiers, port numbers, and machine types.
tldr.outcome: Provides a central reference for protocol parameter assignments, maintained by Joyce Reynolds at USC-ISI. Historic and replaced by RFC 923.

today: RFC 900 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 923 in 1985. These assigned numbers registries were updated periodically, with RFC 960 providing an updated version also published in 1985. The modern Internet now uses hierarchical assignment processes managed by IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) rather than centralized lists like this RFC.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 900 is an official status report on the numbers used in protocols in the ARPA-Internet community. It documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations, with the assignment process managed by Joyce Reynolds at USC-ISI.

The RFC serves as a central registry and explains that network administrators developing new protocols or applications requiring network numbers, links, sockets, or ports should contact Joyce Reynolds for number assignments. The document will be updated periodically as new assignments are made.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an official list saying "these are the numbers we use for different things on the network." If you want a new number, you ask the person in charge.

sections.title: IP Address Classes and Network Numbers
sections.content:
The RFC details three classes of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses. Class A has a 7-bit network number and 24-bit local address, with the highest-order bit set to 0, allowing 128 possible Class A networks. Class B has a 14-bit network number and 16-bit local address with the two highest-order bits set to 1-0, allowing 16,384 Class B networks. Class C has a 21-bit network number and 8-bit local address with three highest-order bits set to 1-1-0, allowing over 2 million Class C networks.

Addresses are written in dotted decimal notation dividing the 32-bit address into four 8-bit fields. Network numbers are assigned to networks connected to the ARPA-Internet and DDN-Internet, with categorization codes (R for Research, D for Defense, G for Government, C for Commercial) placed to the left of the network number.
sections.plainLanguage: IP addresses are split into network numbers and local addresses. Different formats for big networks, medium networks, and small networks. Each organization gets a code showing whether it's research, military, government, or commercial.

sections.title: Protocol Numbers, Versions, and Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC assigns version numbers for Internet Protocol implementations. Version 4 (IPv4) is specified for the standard Internet Protocol, while version 5 is designated for ST Datagram Mode. Versions 0, 15, and 6-14 are reserved or unassigned.

Protocol numbers identify which protocol follows the IP header. Assignments include ICMP (1), GGP (3), TCP (6), UDP (17), EGP (8), and many others. These numbers tell the IP layer which higher-level protocol to pass the data to. Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs) are also assigned for grouping gateways that form autonomous systems in the Exterior Gateway Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Different protocols get different numbers so the computer knows what to do with the data. TCP is one number, UDP is another, and so on. It's like labeling packages with what's inside.

sections.title: Well-Known Port Numbers and Services
sections.content:
The RFC assigns port numbers for TCP and UDP services. Well-known ports include port 21 for FTP (File Transfer Protocol), port 25 for SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), port 23 for TELNET, port 53 for Domain Name Server, and many others. These are the standard contact ports where server processes listen for incoming connections.

The assigned ports use a convention where all except the lowest eight bits are cleared to zero, with the low-order eight bits specified in the tables. The same port assignments are used with UDP where possible, providing consistency across transport protocols. The list reflects both active protocols and experimental or planned protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Services listen on numbered doors called ports. Email uses port 25, web browsing uses port 80, and so on. This list says which service listens on which door.

sections.title: Network Identifiers and Hardware Types
sections.content:
Beyond IP addresses and protocol numbers, the RFC documents Ethernet numbers (message type fields used by Ethernet networks to identify protocols), ARPANET link numbers, IEEE 802 Service Access Points, and ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) parameters. It also lists official machine names and operating system names that were in use with the ARPANET and early Internet.

The document includes network totals showing distribution by user category and network class. Research networks dominated the allocations, with 867 Class A through Class C networks assigned for ARPA-Internet and DDN-Internet use, while independent networks received additional allocations.
sections.plainLanguage: The list includes other numbers too: different networks used different numbering schemes for their messages, and all of those are documented here. It also lists what machines and operating systems existed in 1984.
